title: They walk humbly
hookLine: servants of the Merciful walk gently, and when the ignorant address them, say peace (25:63)

lines: CUT IN LINE, THEN GLARED AT.
cards: Someone cuts in front of you in line, then glares at you as if you'd done it. A stranger online answers a harmless comment with something cruel. A driver leans on the horn and shouts a word you won't repeat.
There's a split second where the body gets ready to answer in kind.
Near its end, Surah Al-Furqan paints a portrait of a certain kind of person, and the first two strokes are about exactly this: how they walk, and what they say when someone is rude to them.

teach.b: Verse sixty-three. The portrait has a title: 'ibad ar-Rahman, the servants of the Most Merciful.
Pickthall calls them the faithful slaves of the Beneficent, "who walk upon the earth modestly, and when the foolish ones address them answer: Peace". Walk modestly is yamshuna hawnan.
Hawn means ease, lightness, gentleness. Not slinking, not timid. Just walking without swagger, without needing the street to notice you.
Then the foolish ones, al-jahilun. Scholars of early Arabic point out that jahl isn't only not knowing things.
It's the opposite of hilm, forbearance. A jahil is someone hot-tempered, rash, quick to insult. So someone flares up at them, and they answer, salaman.
Peace. Commentators read that in more than one way. Some say it means a word of peace, a calm reply that refuses to escalate.
Others say they speak in a way that keeps them safe from sin: something decent, and they move on. Neither reading makes it weakness.
A hadith in Bukhari says the strong person isn't the one who wins at wrestling; the strong one is the one who controls himself when angry. That's the strength in this verse.

The portrait runs on to the end of the surah, and there's more of it ahead. But it begins at street level: how you carry your body down the road, and the first thing you say when someone throws something at you.
The servants of the Merciful get their name from Him. The gentleness is borrowed.

how: Muslim teachers often read 25:63–77, the portrait of 'ibad ar-Rahman, as a description of good character, and quote verse 63 when teaching how to respond to insults.

o: quietly, avoiding every stranger on the road
slowly, with eyes always fixed on the ground
gently, with ease: walking without swagger

games.q: inside the portrait — tap the pairs.

s: walking humbly means walking timidly, eyes down
hawn is ease and gentleness: walking without swagger, not slinking.
in older Arabic, jahl can mean rashness, not only not knowing
it's the opposite of hilm, forbearance.
answering 'peace' is a sign of weakness
a hadith in Bukhari says the strong one is the one who controls himself when angry.

games.q: someone hot-tempered insults you in the street. you're one of the servants of the Merciful. what do you say?
o: nothing, but glare until they leave.
games.why: they answer: peace. commentators read it as a calm word that refuses to escalate, and keeps the speaker clear of wrong.

practice: Remember the last time someone was short with you, and how your body got ready to reply.
Replay it slowly, and this time let your shoulders drop: picture saying something calm and short, peace, okay, have a good day, and walking on, lightly. If you pray, you can ask for that ease.

wordCard.voice: Hawnan. Gently, with ease: how the servants of the Merciful walk the earth, and answer the rash with peace. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: gently, with ease; 25:63 says the servants of the Merciful walk hawnan.

carryVoice: Your line: walk gently; say peace. Strength, here, looks like self-control and a calm reply. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: who walk upon the earth modestly, and when the foolish ones address them answer: Peace

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 6114 (the strong one controls himself in anger)
